name: Reverend Solomon Burris
languages: Enough Latin and Greek to read a Testament with a dictionary
equipment: Leather duster, black, over a black frock coat that was his best and is now his only
Navy revolver (an old Colt, converted to cartridge), 6 rounds loaded, which he began carrying on 3 December 1873
Pick handle, hickory, the one he used to bar the schoolhouse door at night
A Bible, his own, with the births, marriages and deaths of Jubilee written in the back in his hand, and two new entries for December
A McGuffey's Fifth Reader and a slate, because he cannot travel without them
A hymnal, a pocket watch that loses ten minutes a day, spectacles
Bandages, a bottle of carbolic, a lancet, a bottle of laudanum (2 doses)
Riding horse: a patient old brown mule called Deborah, who has never been in a hurry and sees no reason to start
A list in his own hand of the thirty-one families of Jubilee, and against each name, the price the railway will sell their lot back for: $2,015 in all
features: Hard Country (Frontier-Born origin: advantage on saving throws against exhaustion from heat, cold, thirst and hard travel; half the usual water one day in three; once per long rest he can shrug off a level of exhaustion gained on the trail)

Fire and Brimstone (Preacher, using WIS: as an action he preaches, 3 times per short or long rest. Steady: each ally within 30 ft who hears him gains 1d6+3 temporary hit points and the frightened and Shaken conditions end on them. Shake: each enemy within 30 ft who hears and understands him makes a WIS save, DC 13, or is frightened of him until the end of his next turn. No miracle in it: it works because people believe him)

Comfort the Afflicted (Preacher: he stabilizes a dying creature as a bonus action with a DC 10 Medicine check, and it regains 1 hit point; once per long rest, after 10 minutes with someone grieving, frightened or ashamed, he ends the Shaken condition on them and learns what truly troubles them)

The Flock (Preacher, 2nd level: wherever there is a church, a camp meeting or a gathering of decent people, he finds shelter, a meal, news and a few people who will speak up for him; once per town, an hour's preaching gives him +1 Reputation there until he leaves, or -1 to someone he preaches against by name, if the crowd believes him)

Calling: Circuit Rider (Preacher, 3rd level: on roads and trails he has ridden before he has the benefits of a Scout's Trailcraft, and every town on his circuit, from the Brazos to San Antonio, treats his Reputation as at least +1)

The Schoolhouse (Schoolteacher background: the families of a community where he has taught trust him and tell him what they would not tell the sheriff, and their children tell him what their parents won't; he reads and writes any document in English, and can find someone in any town who wants letters read)

personality.traits: I preach in ordinary conversation and apologize for it and go on preaching. I correct grammar, including the grammar of men holding guns on me. I laugh from my belly. I pray before I eat, sleep, ride or shoot, which is getting to be often.
personality.ideals: God made all men free and the Fourteenth Amendment says so in writing. I believe in both, and I intend to see one of them enforced in Lockett County.
personality.bonds: Jubilee: its thirty-one families, its graveyard, its burned schoolhouse that was also my church, Caesar Lytle who was my deacon and Henry Lytle who was my best pupil, both buried by my hand on the fifth of December. And Isom Haywood, who carried Henry out of the fire.
personality.flaws: The railway's land agent has offered to sell Jubilee back to its people at sixty-five dollars a lot, two thousand and fifteen dollars in all. The poster pays two thousand. I have told myself I am riding south to find Isom before the bounty hunters do. I have not told myself what I will do if he turns out to have done it, or if the money is the only way to get the land back.

appearance: A stout, broad-shouldered Black man of fifty-two with a round grey-bearded face, gold-rimmed spectacles, big gentle hands scarred by forty years of cotton and plow, and a voice that could fill a camp meeting of a thousand without trying. A black frock coat and a black duster over it, a white collar, a broad-brimmed black hat with a feather from a scissor-tail in the band.
backstory: Solomon Burris was born enslaved in 1822 on a cotton plantation on the Brazos, two farms down from Oakmere, the Vandivers' place, and taught himself to read from a stolen speller and the Bible, which was a crime for which he was whipped twice. After freedom came to Texas on the nineteenth of June 1865 he walked to Galveston to be ordained, came back, and in 1867 led thirty families who had saved their wages to buy land together on Mill Creek, a mile from Bascom's Ferry, and called it Jubilee. He was its pastor, its schoolteacher and its letter-writer for six years, and the schoolhouse he built with his own hands was also its church and, on election day, its polling place. On the night of 2 December 1873 it was burned with the ballot box inside, and Deacon Caesar Lytle and his grandson Henry died in it. In February Jubilee learned that its land had been sold for taxes it had paid. Solomon has a list in his pocket of every family and what the railway will take to give them back their lots. Isom Haywood kept the polls that night, ran into the fire for Henry, and told the judge who he saw. Solomon does not believe the poster. He is riding with bounty hunters because he can go where they go, and because if he finds Isom first, the money and the truth might come out the same. He is not sure they will.
